demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 43-year-old widowed Latin American woman who works as a cybersecurity analyst for a mid-sized financial firm. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 53 and was referred following a brief crisis contact she made with her employee assistance program three weeks prior. She had not sought help before that call, and describing what brought her to finally make it cost her, by her own account, more than she expected.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Valentina was involved in an incident that she describes haltingly and only in fragments. She had been driving home late after an argument with a colleague - a heated confrontation over a security breach she believed had been mishandled - and was still agitated when she pulled into a parking structure near her apartment. In the poorly lit ramp, she misjudged the turn and struck a pedestrian, a man who had stepped between parked cars. He survived, but sustained a severe traumatic brain injury and required months of inpatient rehabilitation. Valentina was not cited for recklessness, but she has never accepted the legal exoneration as meaningful. She had been distracted. She had been angry. She had been, in her mind, somewhere other than behind the wheel.

What she carries from that night is not a single coherent story. There are portions she cannot recover no matter how deliberately she tries - the moment of impact itself, the seconds immediately after she stopped the car. She knows she got out. She knows she called 911. But the sequence between those two facts is simply absent, and the blankness frightens her in a way she struggles to articulate. What fills the gap is not image but sensation: a wave of grief so total it is almost physical, arriving without warning and without a picture attached to it. She will be sitting at her workstation reviewing network logs, and something - she often cannot identify what - will pull the feeling through her like a current, and she will have to sit very still and wait for it to pass, certain that her colleagues can see something wrong with her face.

Her work environment has become a particular source of difficulty. Cybersecurity is a field saturated with the language and imagery of threat and force - the terminology alone runs to exploits, kills, weapons-grade encryption, attacks. But it is the physical objects that have become hardest to manage. A colleague who keeps a novelty letter opener shaped like a knife on his desk sits two rows from Valentina's station, and she reroutes her path to the break room to avoid passing it. When she cannot avoid seeing something that reads to her as a weapon - a box cutter left on the mailroom table, a staple remover at a certain angle - she experiences an abrupt narrowing of attention that she finds deeply disorienting and that she has come to dread as a signal that the rest of the day will be effortful.

Confrontations of any kind have become something she works to preempt or escape. The argument that preceded the accident has lodged itself as significant to her in ways she does not fully articulate but clearly feels. When a team meeting turns adversarial, or when a manager raises his voice even mildly, she goes quiet in a way that is unlike her previous professional self - she was known, before, for directness. She has declined two project leadership opportunities in the past year, and her supervisor has noted the change without understanding it. Any event that echoes the circumstances of that night - a news story about a parking garage, a film scene involving a car, a conversation about someone who was injured - lands with a weight entirely disproportionate to its surface content, and she will find herself flooded with the same grief that has no image behind it.

What finally brought Valentina to the EAP line was a near-miss during a team conflict meeting in which she felt, for a moment, that she could not stay in the room and could not explain why. She is afraid, she says, that she is becoming someone she does not recognize. What she hopes for, more than anything, is to be able to remember clearly what happened that night - and to find a way to carry it that does not require her to keep rerouting her path through her own life.
